items.quote: Please send us the signed code of conduct and your emergency contact form by 05/06/2026; we cannot confirm your room until we have both.
items.computation: The letter prints the deadline as the numeric date '05/06/2026', which is genuinely ambiguous: read as day/month/year (the convention normally used in Germany, where the sender is based) it means 5 June 2026; read as month/day/year (a convention an English-language international summer school addressing participants abroad might also use) it means 6 May 2026. Nothing else in the letter disambiguates it — the document date '03/03/2026' is day 3 of month 3 either way, so it gives no clue about the sender's convention. No statutory delivery or counting rule applies here since this is a private company's administrative request, not an authority's legally defined deadline, so the printed date (on whichever reading) stands as written with no weekend/holiday shift. Following the instruction to use the earliest plausible reading when a date is genuinely ambiguous, the earliest of the two candidate dates, 6 May 2026, is used, with low confidence and a warning flagging the alternative reading of 5 June 2026.
